> 「汝若作是念：『如来不以具足相故，得阿耨多罗三藐三菩提。』……莫作是念！……发阿耨多罗三藐三菩提心者，于法不说断灭相。」

Section twenty-seven forbids a thought that the previous twenty-six sections have been carefully building toward.

Do not think: *the Tathāgata attained awakening by not having the perfect marks.*

Read that again, because it sounds like the correct conclusion. Marks are empty; the perfected body is not the ground; therefore awakening must be the absence of marks.

The sutra says: no. Do not think that either.

## The negation has a trapdoor

The whole text has been running a machine that removes supports. Each removal is correct. But a machine that removes supports will, if left running unattended, remove the ground of causality as well — and that is not what any of it meant.

The specific error: concluding that because marks are not ultimate, the absence of marks is. Which turns emptiness into a position, and a position is exactly what the sutra has been dissolving.

The book names it 断灭相 — the mark of cutting off. The view that at the end of the analysis everything is abolished: cause and effect, good and evil, the continuity of consequences.

## 于法不说断灭相

A person who has actually aroused the mind of awakening, the text says, does not speak of dharmas as cut off.

This is a statement about what such a person *says*, which is a testable thing. Listen to how someone talks about emptiness. If the vocabulary of abolition keeps appearing — nothing matters, no one is really there, consequences are illusory — the section's diagnosis applies.

## 无断 is not 无灭 only

The pair matters. 无断: the continuity is not severed. 无灭: nothing is extinguished into nullity.

Both deny the same error from two sides: causes continue to produce effects; appearances continue to appear; the person who understands this does not thereby become exempt from it.

And both are compatible with the earlier negations, because the earlier negations were about *substance*, not about *function*. A thing can lack own-nature and still function completely. That is the sentence the whole sutra has been circling.

## The failure mode in practice

The book describes it plainly: a person who has understood non-abiding, and then uses the understanding as permission.

Permission for what? For carelessness, usually. For not answering, not repairing, not staying. The reasoning is always a version of "it is all empty anyway", delivered in the tone of someone who has seen through something.

The twenty-seventh section says this is not a misunderstanding of the details. It is a failure at the level of the vow — an awakening mind that speaks of cutting off has, at that moment, stopped being an awakening mind.

## The test

Listen to yourself explain emptiness to someone. Or recall the last time you did.

Was there a sentence in it that amounted to "so it does not matter"? Something that made the listener's obligation lighter, or yours?

If so, you were speaking 断灭相, and this section was written for exactly that sentence.
